etymology: English evangelical clergyman (1816-1900), first Anglican Bishop of Liverpool, author of Holiness and Expository Thoughts on the Gospels.
biblical_def: John Charles Ryle was an English evangelical clergyman and the first Bishop of Liverpool, one of the clearest and most pointed gospel writers of the nineteenth century. Converted as a young man through hearing the Scriptures read in church, he gave his life to plain, earnest, doctrinally Reformed preaching and writing aimed at the conscience of ordinary people. His tracts and books, written in short, vigorous, unmistakable sentences, reached vast numbers. His best-known work, Holiness, defends the biblical doctrine of progressive sanctification by the Spirit through ongoing struggle against sin, over against the "higher life" teaching that promised an effortless victory by simple surrender. He also wrote Practical Religion, Old Paths, and the much-loved Expository Thoughts on the Gospels. Ryle was a convinced Protestant and evangelical who contended for justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, and the necessity of conversion, while warning against ritualism and liberalism alike. Ryle stands in the dictionary as the plain-spoken bishop of gospel clarity, who taught the church that true holiness is a lifelong fight of faith, not a single crisis of surrender, and who pressed the great truths of the gospel upon the conscience with a directness few have matched.
webster_summary: English evangelical clergyman (1816-1900), first Bishop of Liverpool; author of Holiness and Expository Thoughts on the Gospels, who defended progressive sanctification by the Spirit and pressed the gospel on the conscience with plain, pointed clarity.

scriptures: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
...work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
corruption_summary: Ryle's Holiness corrects the "higher life" error of effortless sanctification by surrender, recovering the biblical doctrine of holiness as a lifelong fight of faith empowered by the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Effortless-victory correction. The "higher life" or "let go and let God" teaching promised instant, effortless holiness through a single act of surrender. Ryle answered from Scripture that sanctification is a lifelong battle: the believer must "fight the good fight of faith" (1 Tim 6:12) and "work out" his salvation, even as God works in him (Phil 2:12-13). The dictionary holds that holiness is real, progressive, and hard-won by the Spirit's power through diligent struggle, not a shortcut that bypasses the warfare every Christian is called to wage.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the necessity of holiness itself. Ryle insisted that "holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Heb 12:14) is not optional. The dictionary commends his warning against a cheap grace that severs justification from sanctification: those truly justified by faith will pursue holiness, and a professed faith that produces no growth in godliness is a faith to be examined, not assumed.

etymology: English-born Reformed teacher and writer (1886-1952), author of The Sovereignty of God and The Attributes of God.
biblical_def: Arthur Walkington Pink was an English-born Bible teacher and writer who, through his monthly magazine Studies in the Scriptures and a host of books, helped recover the doctrines of sovereign grace in the twentieth century. Converted out of a brief involvement with the occult, he became a fervent preacher and then, increasingly, a writer reaching a small circle in his lifetime but a vast readership after his death, when his works were reprinted and widely circulated. His best-known book, The Sovereignty of God, sets forth God's absolute rule over creation, providence, and salvation with uncompromising force; his The Attributes of God, The Holy Spirit, and many expository works pressed the same God-centered vision. Pink wrote against the man-centered, decisional, and shallow tendencies of the religion of his day, recalling readers to the majesty of God, the depravity of man, and the freeness of sovereign grace. Pink stands in the dictionary as a twentieth-century recoverer of God-centered theology, who taught the church to bow before the sovereignty and the glorious attributes of God, and whose writings, little regarded in his lifetime, became a means of reviving Reformed conviction across the English-speaking world.
webster_summary: English-born Reformed teacher and writer (1886-1952), author of The Sovereignty of God and The Attributes of God; little known in life but widely read after his death, he helped recover God-centered theology in the twentieth century.

scriptures: But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.

corruption_summary: Pink's work corrects a man-centered religion that dethrones God in favor of human will, recovering the biblical vision of God's absolute sovereignty over all things, including salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: Man-centered correction. The religion of Pink's day, like ours, often made man the center and measure, reducing God to a helper who waits on the human will. Pink recalled the church to the throne: "our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased" (Psa 115:3). The dictionary holds the sovereignty of God over creation, providence, and salvation, against every theology that enthrones the creature and shrinks the Creator to a manageable, man-serving deity.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the God-centeredness of all true theology. Pink's lifelong burden was that God be seen as God — sovereign, holy, and glorious in all His attributes — and that man be humbled before Him. The dictionary commends this vision: God works all things after the counsel of His own will (Eph 1:11), and the recovery of His sovereignty is the recovery of worship, for only the great God of Scripture is worthy of the awe and adoration He demands.

etymology: English and American evangelical minister (1808-1878), "the pilgrim's companion," author of warm experiential devotional works.
biblical_def: Octavius Winslow was a nineteenth-century evangelical minister who labored in both America and England, beloved as one of the warmest and most Christ-centered devotional writers of his age. A preacher of the doctrines of grace, he is remembered chiefly for books that bring the comforts of the gospel to the believing heart in its trials, declensions, and sorrows. His Personal Declension and Revival of Religion in the Soul traces the subtle ways a Christian's love may grow cold and the path of recovery; his Morning Thoughts and Evening Thoughts furnished daily meditations savored by generations; and works like The Precious Things of God and No Condemnation in Christ Jesus dwell on the riches of union with Christ and the security of the believer. Winslow wrote always to exalt Christ and to console and search the soul, joining doctrinal soundness to deep tenderness. He stands in the dictionary as the pilgrim's companion in experiential devotion, who taught the church that the doctrines of grace are not cold abstractions but warm springs of comfort, and who pointed the declining, the grieving, and the doubting soul afresh to the all-sufficiency and tender love of Christ.
webster_summary: English and American evangelical minister (1808-1878), a warm Christ-centered devotional writer; author of Personal Declension and Revival of Religion in the Soul and Morning Thoughts, who brought the comforts of the gospel to the trial-worn heart.

scriptures: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.

corruption_summary: Winslow's writings honor the recovery of experiential religion — the doctrines of grace felt and enjoyed in the heart — against both a cold orthodoxy and a shallow cheer that knows nothing of the soul's declensions and revivals.
corruption_paragraphs: Cold-orthodoxy correction. Sound doctrine can be held in a cold and lifeless way, never warming the affections. Winslow refused that divorce, pressing the comforts of the gospel upon the heart: there is now no condemnation to them in Christ (Rom 8:1), and the Shepherd restores the soul (Psa 23:3). The dictionary holds that the doctrines of grace are meant to be experienced, and commends Winslow's tender application of truth to the believer's actual griefs, declensions, and fears.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reality of spiritual declension and revival in the believer's own soul. Winslow charted how a Christian's first love may cool (Rev 2:4) and how it may be revived, refusing the shallow assumption that the believer's walk is always steady and bright. The dictionary commends his realism and his hope: the people of God do decline, but the Shepherd who carries the lambs in His bosom (Isa 40:11) restores the soul, and there is a way back to first love.

etymology: Scottish Reformed layman, philanthropist, and theologian (1764-1842), author of an Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans and catalyst of the Geneva revival.
biblical_def: Robert Haldane was a wealthy Scottish landowner who, converted to a vital evangelical faith, devoted his fortune and his energies to the spread of the gospel, and became, with his brother James, a leading figure of revival in Scotland and beyond. Selling his estate to fund missions and gospel work, he supported preachers, founded churches, and labored for the conversion of the lost. His most famous and far-reaching service came during a visit to Geneva and Montauban, where he gathered theological students — many of them spiritually dead in the rationalism of the day — and taught them through the Epistle to the Romans verse by verse. Under that teaching a number were soundly converted, including men like Merle d'Aubigné, César Malan, and Frédéric Monod, who became leaders of the evangelical "Réveil" (Awakening) across French-speaking Europe. Out of those studies came Haldane's massive Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, a rich and thorough commentary on the doctrines of grace. Haldane stands in the dictionary as the layman who sparked the Geneva revival, who proved that the patient teaching of the Epistle to the Romans can raise the spiritually dead, and whose stewardship of wealth and gifts for the gospel is a pattern of consecrated means.
webster_summary: Scottish Reformed layman and theologian (1764-1842), author of an Exposition of Romans; who sold his estate for the gospel and, by teaching Romans to Geneva students, sparked the evangelical "Réveil" across French-speaking Europe.

corruption_summary: Haldane's life honors the recovery of Romans as the power of God to raise the spiritually dead, and of the consecrated stewardship of wealth for the gospel, against a dead rationalism and a hoarding of means.
corruption_paragraphs: Rationalism correction. The Geneva students Haldane taught had been schooled in a rationalism that emptied the gospel of its power. By simply opening the Epistle to the Romans, Haldane saw the dead made alive. The dictionary holds that the gospel of Romans is "the power of God unto salvation" (Rom 1:16); no human academy or system can substitute for the plain teaching of the Word, which alone raises the spiritually dead and revives the church.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the stewardship of wealth and gifts for the kingdom. Haldane sold his estate and poured his fortune into gospel work, a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7) rich in good works (1 Tim 6:18). The dictionary commends his example against a hoarding spirit: what God entrusts to His people is to be held loosely and spent freely for His glory and the salvation of souls, as Haldane spent his all.

etymology: American Baptist theologian (1794-1884), author of the first systematic theology written by a Southern Baptist, his Manual of Theology.
biblical_def: John Leadley Dagg was an American Baptist pastor, educator, and theologian, remembered as the author of the first full systematic theology produced among Southern Baptists, his Manual of Theology (1857), with its companion Manual of Church Order. Largely self-taught, and afflicted through much of his life with failing eyesight and bodily weakness that eventually left him nearly blind, Dagg nonetheless became one of the most respected theological minds of his denomination. His Manual of Theology is marked by clarity, devotional warmth, and a thoroughly Reformed and Baptist account of the doctrines of grace, the person and work of Christ, and the Christian life; it opens, characteristically, by grounding all theology in the love of God and the duty of love to Him. Dagg's humility and piety were as notable as his learning; he wrote as a worshiper, not merely a scholar. He stands in the dictionary as the pioneer systematic theologian of the Baptists, who showed that careful doctrine and warm devotion belong together, who bore lifelong infirmity with patient faith, and whose Manual of Theology set the doctrines of grace before the church in language at once exact, accessible, and adoring.
webster_summary: American Baptist theologian (1794-1884), author of the first Southern Baptist systematic theology, the Manual of Theology; a largely self-taught, nearly blind, deeply pious writer who joined Reformed doctrine to devotional warmth.

corruption_summary: Dagg's work honors the recovery of theology grounded in the love of God and married to devotion, and of patient faith under affliction, against a cold academic divinity and an impatience with weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: Love-less-theology correction. Theology can be pursued as a cold intellectual exercise, divorced from the love of God it ought to serve. Dagg began his Manual with the great commandment, grounding all doctrine in loving God with heart, soul, and mind (Matt 22:37). The dictionary holds that the end of theology is the love and worship of God; the soundest doctrine, rightly held, kindles love, for he that loveth not knoweth not God (1 John 4:8), and Dagg wrote his theology as an act of devotion.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is patient faith under affliction. Dagg labored through failing eyesight and weakness, eventually nearly blind, yet produced works of lasting worth. The dictionary commends his example: God's grace is sufficient and His strength made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9), and the afflicted servant who learns God's statutes in the furnace (Psa 119:71) often bears the richest fruit, his very weakness a stage for the power of God.

etymology: American Presbyterian theologian (1772-1851), first professor of Princeton Theological Seminary and father of Old Princeton.
biblical_def: Archibald Alexander was an American Presbyterian minister and theologian, the first professor of Princeton Theological Seminary when it was founded in 1812, and the father of the "Old Princeton" theology that would shape American Reformed thought for a century through him and his successors, the Hodges and Warfield. A man of warm experiential piety as well as careful learning, Alexander combined rigorous Reformed orthodoxy with a deep concern for the reality of religion in the heart. His enduring work, Thoughts on Religious Experience, traces the marks of genuine conversion and the course of the Christian life with rare spiritual discernment, helping believers distinguish true grace from its counterfeits and guiding the anxious soul. He trained generations of ministers, insisting that sound doctrine and vital godliness must go together, and that the seminary existed to produce not merely scholars but holy and useful pastors. Alexander stands in the dictionary as the founder of Old Princeton and a physician of religious experience, who joined confessional Reformed theology to experiential warmth, and who taught the church that orthodoxy and heartfelt piety are not rivals but partners, both necessary to a faithful ministry and a healthy soul.
webster_summary: American Presbyterian theologian (1772-1851), first professor of Princeton Seminary and father of Old Princeton; author of Thoughts on Religious Experience, who joined confessional Reformed orthodoxy to experiential warmth.

scriptures: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves...
Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

corruption_summary: Alexander's legacy honors the union of confessional orthodoxy and experiential piety, against both a dead orthodoxy without heart-religion and an emotionalism without doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Orthodoxy-without-life correction. Confessional precision can harden into a religion of the head alone. Alexander insisted that true religion must be experienced in the heart: men must be born again (John 3:7), and the gospel comes not in word only but in power and the Holy Ghost (1 Thess 1:5). The dictionary holds, with Old Princeton at its best, that sound doctrine and vital godliness belong together; the seminary and the church need not choose between orthodoxy and experience, but must hold both.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discernment of genuine religious experience. Alexander's great work helped believers examine themselves (2 Cor 13:5), distinguishing true conversion from its many imitations. The dictionary commends this pastoral wisdom against both a presumptuous assurance and a groundless despair: there are marks of genuine grace, the soul may and should be examined, and the faithful pastor, like Alexander, helps his people know whether they are truly in the faith.

etymology: American evangelist (1783-1844) of the Second Great Awakening, defender of doctrinally grounded revival against manipulative "new measures."
biblical_def: Asahel Nettleton was an American evangelist of the Second Great Awakening, remarkable both for the depth and durability of his converts and for his principled opposition to the manipulative revivalism that arose in his day. A convinced Calvinist, Nettleton preached the sovereignty of God, the depravity of man, and the necessity of the Spirit's work, and labored with great care for genuine conversions; the fruit of his ministry was notable for its soundness and permanence, with comparatively few of his converts falling away. When Charles Finney introduced the "new measures" — the anxious bench, emotional pressure, and techniques designed to produce immediate decisions — Nettleton opposed them, warning that such methods manufactured false conversions and confused the work of man with the work of God. He insisted that true revival is the sovereign work of the Holy Spirit, not a result that can be engineered by technique. Nettleton stands in the dictionary as the evangelist of sound revival, who labored for conversions wrought by the Spirit and grounded in truth, and who warned the church that manipulation and emotional pressure, however effective at producing decisions, cannot produce the new birth, which is the work of God alone.

corruption_summary: Nettleton's ministry corrects a manipulative revivalism that manufactures decisions by technique, recovering the truth that the new birth is the sovereign, un-engineered work of the Holy Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Manufactured-decisions correction. The "new measures" Nettleton opposed used emotional pressure and technique to produce immediate decisions, confusing human persuasion with divine regeneration. Nettleton held that the new birth is of God, not of the will of man (John 1:13), and that the Spirit, like the wind, blows where He wills (John 3:8). The dictionary holds that genuine conversion cannot be engineered; decisionism that manufactures professions by manipulation produces false converts, and the church must labor for the Spirit-wrought new birth, not for counted hands.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that revival is God's work, not man's technique. "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit" (Zech 4:6); neither he that plants nor he that waters is anything, but God who gives the increase (1 Cor 3:7). The dictionary commends Nettleton's patient, prayerful, doctrinally grounded labor against every method that trusts in human means to produce what only the Spirit can give, and honors the soundness and permanence of conversions truly wrought by God.

etymology: American Presbyterian theologian (1823-1886), son of Charles Hodge and a Princeton professor, author of Outlines of Theology.
biblical_def: Archibald Alexander Hodge — named for the founder of Princeton Seminary — was an American Presbyterian theologian, the son of the great Charles Hodge, whom he succeeded as professor of theology at Princeton. Heir to the Old Princeton tradition, he was a gifted teacher and a clear, accessible systematic theologian. His best-known work, Outlines of Theology, set forth the whole of Reformed doctrine in a lucid question-and-answer and expository form that made it a favorite handbook for students and ministers; his commentary The Confession of Faith expounded the Westminster Confession with the same clarity. With Benjamin Warfield he co-authored an influential essay on the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture, defending the full trustworthiness of the Bible against rising critical attacks. A. A. Hodge combined his father's confessional orthodoxy with a warm and vivid teaching style, and was known for his pithy, memorable expressions of doctrine. He stands in the dictionary as the clear teacher of Old Princeton, who made the riches of Reformed systematic theology accessible to ordinary students, defended the inerrancy of Scripture, and carried forward the confessional, God-centered tradition of Princeton into the latter nineteenth century.
webster_summary: American Presbyterian theologian (1823-1886), son of Charles Hodge and a Princeton professor; author of Outlines of Theology and a defender, with Warfield, of biblical inerrancy, who made Reformed systematic theology clear and accessible.

scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:

corruption_summary: A. A. Hodge's work honors the recovery of clear, confessional systematic theology and the defense of biblical inerrancy, against both a doctrinal vagueness and the higher-critical assault on Scripture's trustworthiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Higher-criticism correction. In Hodge's day the higher criticism was beginning its assault on the inspiration and trustworthiness of Scripture. With Warfield, Hodge defended the full inspiration and inerrancy of the Bible: all Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16), given as holy men were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Pet 1:21), and the Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). The dictionary holds the inerrancy of the written Word against every critical theory that would lodge error in the text God Himself inspired.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the value of clear, accessible systematic theology. Hodge's Outlines made the whole of Reformed doctrine graspable for ordinary students. The dictionary commends such labor: the deep truths of the faith are not to be locked in the academy but set in clear order for the church, that the simple might be made wise (Psa 19:7) and every believer grounded in the doctrine once delivered to the saints.
roots_summary: American Presbyterian theologian (1823-1886), son of Charles Hodge and a Princeton professor; author of Outlines of Theology and a defender of inerrancy with Warfield.

etymology: American Presbyterian pastor (1785-1873) of the Brick Church in New York City, author of The Distinguishing Traits of Christian Character.
biblical_def: Gardiner Spring was an American Presbyterian minister who served the Brick Presbyterian Church in New York City for more than sixty years, a long and influential pastorate spanning much of the nineteenth century. A faithful preacher of evangelical and Reformed conviction, he wrote a number of devotional and doctrinal works that were widely read in his day. His The Distinguishing Traits of Christian Character set forth the marks by which genuine saving faith may be known, helping professing believers examine whether their religion was real; his The Attraction of the Cross lifted up the crucified Christ as the great magnet of the soul; and his The Power of the Pulpit addressed the high calling of preaching. Spring also gave his name to the "Gardiner Spring Resolutions," a controversial measure during the Civil War. As a pastor he labored for the conversion and growth of his large flock through decades of change. Gardiner Spring stands in the dictionary as the long-serving pastor of distinguishing grace, who helped the church discern the marks of true Christian character, who held up the cross of Christ as the soul's great attraction, and whose enduring pastorate witnessed to the worth of faithful, settled ministry over a lifetime.
webster_summary: American Presbyterian pastor (1785-1873) of New York's Brick Church for over sixty years; author of The Distinguishing Traits of Christian Character and The Attraction of the Cross, who helped believers discern the marks of genuine faith.

scriptures: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves...
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.
And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments.
Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
corruption_summary: Spring's work honors the recovery of self-examination and the marks of true faith, and the cross as the soul's great attraction, against a presumptuous religion that never tests itself and a preaching that obscures the crucified Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Presumption correction. Many profess faith without ever examining whether their faith is real. Spring's Distinguishing Traits set forth the marks of genuine Christian character, calling the professor to test himself. The dictionary holds the apostolic command, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5); true faith bears distinguishing fruit (Matt 7:20), and the church is to help its members discern between living faith and dead profession, neither presuming nor despairing but proving themselves.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cross as the soul's great attraction. Spring lifted up the crucified Christ, who said, "if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me" (John 12:32). The dictionary commends the centrality of the cross in preaching: it is not technique, novelty, or eloquence that draws sinners, but Christ crucified held up before them; the faithful pulpit makes the cross its great theme and the magnet of the soul.

etymology: American Presbyterian pastor and theologian (1802-1880), author of commentaries on the Psalms and Romans and of The Grace of Christ.
biblical_def: William Swan Plumer was an American Presbyterian pastor, professor, and writer, a man of imposing presence and warm evangelical conviction who served churches and seminaries across the South and produced a steady stream of devotional and expository works. A faithful preacher of the doctrines of grace, he is remembered especially for his rich expository commentaries, including major works on the Psalms and on the Epistle to the Romans, which combine careful exposition with pastoral and devotional application. He also wrote The Grace of Christ, on the riches of redemption; Vital Godliness; and works on the Ten Commandments and on the providence of God, including reflections on Jehovah-Jireh, the LORD who provides. Plumer's writing is marked by clarity, scriptural saturation, and a constant aim at the edification of the soul. He stands in the dictionary as an expositor of the Psalms and of grace, who fed the church with rich, devotional commentary on the Word, who pressed the doctrines of sovereign grace upon the heart, and who taught believers to trust the providence of the God who sees and provides for His people in every need.
webster_summary: American Presbyterian pastor and theologian (1802-1880), author of major expository commentaries on the Psalms and Romans and of The Grace of Christ; a preacher of sovereign grace who fed the church with rich devotional exposition.

corruption_summary: Plumer's work honors the recovery of rich devotional exposition of Scripture and trust in the providence of the God who provides, against a shallow handling of the Word and an anxious distrust of God's care.
corruption_paragraphs: Shallow-exposition correction. The Word can be handled superficially, mined for quick lessons without patient exposition. Plumer's commentaries on the Psalms and Romans model a richer way: careful, verse-by-verse exposition joined to devotional and pastoral application. The dictionary holds that the Scriptures reward deep, prayerful study — "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" (Psa 119:18) — and commends Plumer's example of feeding the church with rich, edifying exposition of the whole Word.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is trust in the providence of the God who provides. Plumer dwelt on Jehovah-Jireh, "the LORD will provide" (Gen 22:14), and on the promise that all things work together for good to them that love God (Rom 8:28). The dictionary commends this confidence against an anxious, distrustful heart: the God who provided the ram for Abraham still sees and supplies His people's every need, and orders all their circumstances for their good and His glory.
